civilizations: Modern global; ancient Chinese cuju relatives for feet
Multiple; modern toy via Philippines / US

games.name: Chess
games.description: Chess evolved from chaturanga, a war-simulation of infantry, cavalry, elephants, and chariots. As it traveled through Persia (shatranj) into the Islamic world and medieval Europe, pieces became court ranks. The modern queen and bishop powers crystallized in late medieval Europe. Across cultures it has stood for intellect, foresight, and educated leisure.
howToPlay: Orient the board so each player has a light square on the right-hand corner.
Place pieces on the back rank (rook, knight, bishop, queen on her color, king, bishop, knight, rook) with pawns on the second rank.
White moves first; players alternate moving one piece (except when castling).
Capture by landing on an opponent's piece. Win by checkmating the king.
Use special moves when legal: castling, en passant, and pawn promotion.

variations.name: Chaturanga
variations.notes: Ancestral form; elephants instead of bishops; some early accounts mention dice.

variations.name: Shatranj
variations.notes: Persian-Arabic form with firzan (weak queen) and alfil (leaping bishop).

variations.name: Makruk
variations.notes: Thai chess cousin with different piece powers and promotion rules.

variations.name: Sittuyin
variations.notes: Burmese chess with free setup behind the pawns.

games.name: Go (Weiqi)
games.description: Go is an encirclement game of territory. Stones never move once placed; captured groups are removed. One of the Four Arts of the Chinese scholar, it spread to Korea (baduk) and Japan (igo). Play encodes balance, influence, and living shape rather than direct capture of a king.
howToPlay: Black places the first stone on a grid intersection.
Players alternate placing one stone; stones do not move after placement.
A group without liberties (empty adjacent intersections) is captured and removed.
Do not recreate the previous full-board position (ko) or play suicidal moves unless they capture.
When both pass, score territory plus captives (rules vary by country); higher score wins.

variations.name: Baduk
variations.notes: Korean tradition with the same core rules and distinct teaching culture.

variations.name: Igo
variations.notes: Japanese professional ranks and territory scoring conventions.

games.name: Xiangqi
games.description: Xiangqi (Chinese chess) arrays generals, advisors, elephants, horses, chariots, cannons, and soldiers on a lined board crossed by a river. The cannon’s jumping capture and palace confinement give it a tactical flavor distinct from international chess. It remains a beloved park and street game across China.
howToPlay: Arrange pieces on starting points on opposite sides of the river.
Red moves first; pieces move on points according to their type.
Cannons slide like chariots but capture only by jumping over exactly one screen.
Generals stay in the palace; opposing generals may not face on an open file.
Checkmate or stalemate the opposing general to win.
requirements: Xiangqi board with river and palaces

variations.name: Janggi
variations.notes: Korean cousin without a river and with different elephant/horse moves.

games.name: Shogi
games.description: Shogi is Japanese chess distinguished by drops: captured pieces return as your own. Wedge-shaped pieces point toward the opponent. Material swings and dense midgames define its drama; professional shogi remains a major Japanese mind sport.
howToPlay: Set pieces with pointed ends facing the opponent.
Sente moves first—move or drop one piece per turn.
Captured pieces go to your stand and may be dropped later on empty squares (with pawn/check restrictions).
Promote eligible pieces in the last three ranks.
Checkmate the opposing king to win.

variations.name: Chu shogi
variations.notes: Larger historical variant with many unique piece types.

games.name: Mancala sowing games
games.description: Mancala is a family of sowing games: players distribute seeds around pits carved in wood, stone, or earth. Boards appear across Africa, the Middle East, and South Asia. Regional names and pit counts differ, but the scoop-and-sow gesture unites them as one fundamental game with many cultural faces.
howToPlay: Default to a Kalah-style 2×6 board: place four seeds in each of the twelve small pits; leave both end stores empty.
On your turn, scoop all seeds from one pit on your side and sow one seed into each following pit counterclockwise, including your store but skipping the opponent’s store.
If the last seed lands in your store, take another turn; if it lands in an empty pit on your side, capture that seed plus any seeds in the opposite pit into your store.
When one player’s six pits are empty, the opponent moves all remaining seeds into their store and the game ends.
Count seeds in each store; the higher total wins (ties are draws).
requirements: Board with two or more rows of pits

variations.name: Oware
variations.notes: Akan 2×6 classic; capture opposite seeds when ending with 2 or 3.

variations.name: Bao
variations.notes: Complex 4-row Swahili coast game with a special nyumba pit.

variations.name: Congkak
variations.notes: Boat-shaped Southeast Asian board with large stores.

variations.name: Gebeta
variations.notes: Horn of Africa sowing boards.

variations.name: Pallanguzhi
variations.notes: Tamil / South Indian cup-board sowing game.

variations.name: Ayoayo
variations.notes: Yoruba sowing form with rhythmic scooping play.

variations.name: Kalah
variations.notes: Modern commercial teaching form of mancala.

games.name: Backgammon
games.creationYear: c. 2000 BCE ancestors; modern form later
games.description: Race-and-hit dice games stretch from the Royal Game of Ur to Persian nard and European tables. Backgammon blends luck and skill as players bear off fifteen checkers while hitting blots. The doubling cube is a modern strategic layer.
howToPlay: Set checkers in the standard opening formation on the 24 points.
Roll two dice and move checkers forward using both numbers.
Hit a lone opposing blot to the bar; it must re-enter before other moves.
Stack your own checkers for safety; six consecutive points form a prime.
When all fifteen are home, bear off; first to bear off all wins.

variations.name: Nard
variations.notes: Persian tables game closely related to backgammon.

variations.name: Tavli
variations.notes: Greek suite: Portes, Plakoto, Fevga.

variations.name: Shesh Besh
variations.notes: Regional café culture name for backgammon-like play.

variations.name: Royal Game of Ur
variations.notes: Ancient race ancestor with a unique track.

games.name: Senet
games.description: Senet appears in tomb paintings and burial goods across pharaonic Egypt. It held religious meaning as a passage through the afterlife. Exact rules are reconstructed by Egyptologists from later texts and board geometry.
howToPlay: Place pawns on the opening squares of the 30-square track.
Throw sticks or knucklebones for move length.
Advance along the serpentine path; heed special squares (safe, water, rebirth).
Resolve landings on opponents per the reconstruction you follow.
First to bear all pawns off the final squares wins.

games.name: Patolli
games.description: Patolli was a sacred Aztec race game on an X-shaped track using beans as dice. Gambling and ritual offerings intertwined; the game appears in codices and Spanish accounts as cosmic risk made playable.
howToPlay: Lay out the X-shaped board and place markers at the start.
Throw marked beans for a move value.
Advance along the track; honor special spaces and capture rules.
Optional historical wagers can be replaced with points today.
First to complete the circuit with all markers wins.

variations.name: Bul
variations.notes: Related Mesoamerican race/dice tradition.

games.name: Pachisi
games.description: Pachisi—the ‘national game of India’—is a cross-and-circle race traditionally played with cowries. Chaupar is a courtly relative. British Ludo and American Parcheesi are commercial descendants of the same fundamental race.
howToPlay: Each player sits at an arm of the cross with four pieces in nest.
Throw cowries or dice; enter pieces when the throw allows.
Move around the track; safe squares protect stacks.
Landing on a lone opponent sends them home.
First to bring all four pieces into the center wins.

variations.name: Chaupar
variations.notes: Courtly relative with longer arms and dice sticks.

variations.name: Ludo
variations.notes: British patented simplification with cubic dice.

variations.name: Parcheesi
variations.notes: American commercial adaptation.

variations.name: Mensch ärgere dich nicht
variations.notes: German family race game in the same lineage.

games.name: Mahjong
games.description: Mahjong draws on earlier Chinese card and gambling-tile traditions. Four players build melds toward a complete hand while reading discards. Regional styles differ in scoring, but the shuffling ‘wall’ is shared cultural theater.
howToPlay: Build and join four tile walls; break with dice.
Deal hands (usually 13 tiles; dealer 14). East discards first.
Draw or claim a discard for a meld, then discard.
Form chows, pungs, kongs, and a pair.
Declare mahjong on a complete hand; score by regional rules.

variations.name: Riichi mahjong
variations.notes: Closed-hand riichi, dora, strict scoring.

variations.name: Hong Kong mahjong
variations.notes: Fast, pung-oriented popular style.

variations.name: American mahjong
variations.notes: NMJL card hands and jokers.

games.name: Dominoes
games.description: Chinese dominoes relate to dice face pairs; European double-six sets spread via Italy and France. Blocking, scoring, and train games all share matching pip ends—one tool, many table cultures.
howToPlay: Shuffle face-down and draw hands.
Lead with a double or highest tile per the variant.
Play a tile matching an open end, or draw/pass if you cannot.
Place doubles crosswise in most styles.
Win by emptying your hand or reaching a pip score.

variations.name: Mexican Train
variations.notes: Double-twelve party game with personal trains.

variations.name: Draw Dominoes
variations.notes: Common parlor blocking/draw rules.

games.name: Nine Men's Morris
games.description: Mills games form three-in-a-row to capture. Boards are cut into cloister benches across medieval Europe. Southern African morabaraba is the same fundamental mills contest with pastoral ‘cow’ metaphors—catalogued here as variations, not separate inventions.
howToPlay: Place pieces alternately on empty points until all nine are down.
Move along lines to adjacent points.
Form a mill (three in a row) to remove an opposing piece not in a mill if possible.
When down to three pieces, flying jumps to any empty point are often allowed.
Win by reducing the opponent to two pieces or blocking all moves.

variations.name: Morabaraba
variations.notes: Southern African mills with 12 cows per side; school sport form.

variations.name: Umlabalaba
variations.notes: Zulu name for the same mills game.

variations.name: Twelve Men's Morris
variations.notes: Larger piece-count mills variant.

games.name: Alquerque / Draughts family
games.description: Alquerque’s leaping captures on a lined board are documented in Alfonso X’s Book of Games. European draughts/checkers moved the idea onto a checkered board. Saharan kharbaga and related Maghreb games belong to the same leap-capture family—variations of one hunting geometry.
howToPlay: Array pieces on opposing sides.
Move to an adjacent empty point along a line (or dark square in checkers).
Leap an adjacent enemy into an empty landing square to capture.
Continue multi-jumps when allowed.
Capture all enemies or immobilize them to win.
requirements: Lined Alquerque board or checkered draughts board

variations.name: English draughts / checkers
variations.notes: 8×8 checkered form; men move diagonally.

variations.name: International draughts
variations.notes: 10×10 board with flying kings.

variations.name: Kharbaga
variations.notes: Saharan leap-capture relative.

games.name: Fanorona
games.description: Fanorona is Madagascar’s national board game of approach and withdrawal captures. Cascading line captures create sharp tactics. Oral history links boards to royal politics and community rivalry.
howToPlay: Fill the board except the center; white moves first.
Move one piece to an adjacent empty point along a line.
Capture by approach or withdrawal relative to an enemy group.
Continue capturing with the same piece when further captures exist.
Capture all opposing pieces to win.

games.name: Carrom
games.description: Carrom is a tabletop striking game beloved across South Asia and the diaspora. Players flick a striker to pocket carrom men, with the queen requiring a cover. It blends billiards geometry with sitting-room sociability.
howToPlay: Powder the board lightly; place pieces in the center with the queen in the middle.
Flick the striker from your base line to hit your color into pockets.
Pocket the queen, then cover it by pocketing one of your pieces immediately after.
Fouls return pieces or cost turns per rule set.
Clear your pieces (with queen covered) to win.

variations.name: Karrom variant rules (Southeast Asia)
variations.notes: Local foul and scoring house rules on the same board.

games.name: Playing cards (French-suited deck)
games.description: Playing cards likely descended from Chinese money-card ideas and entered Europe via Mamluk decks. French suits became a global standard tool for thousands of games. Regional decks are variations of the same portable gaming platform—not wholly separate toys.
howToPlay: Use a 52-card French-suited deck; shuffle, then deal thirteen cards to each of four players for a Hearts-style starter game.
Play proceeds clockwise; lead any suit except hearts until hearts are broken; players must follow suit if able.
Highest card of the led suit wins the trick; hearts score 1 penalty point each and the queen of spades scores 13.
After all thirteen tricks, tally penalty points; rotate the dealer clockwise for the next hand.
Play hands until one player reaches 100 penalty points; the lowest score wins (or switch later to whist, rummy, or another named game).

variations.name: Italian-suited deck
variations.notes: Cups, coins, swords, batons.

variations.name: German-suited deck
variations.notes: Hearts, bells, acorns, leaves.

variations.name: Spanish baraja
variations.notes: 40- or 48-card decks for mus, tute, etc.

games.name: Hanafuda / Karuta
games.description: Japanese karuta traditions include seasonal hanafuda and literary uta-garuta. Competitive poem-card karuta demands lightning recognition; hanafuda underpins koi-koi. Cards fuse seasons, poetry, and speed into one family of play objects.
howToPlay: For uta-garuta: a reader chants the first half of a poem.
Players race to slap the matching ending card.
Take the card and continue through the set.
For hanafuda/koi-koi: deal, capture by matching months, and declare yaku.
Agree which karuta family you are playing before dealing.

variations.name: Hanafuda
variations.notes: 12-month flower cards.

variations.name: Uta-garuta
variations.notes: One hundred poem-card matching race.

games.name: Ganjifa
games.description: Ganjifa are circular painted cards of Mughal and regional Indian courts, later folk-crafted in places such as Odisha. Suit systems (Mughal, Dashavatara) differ, but trick-taking court hierarchies unite them as one painted-card tradition.
howToPlay: Use an 8-suit Mughal ganjifa set (96 circular cards) or a 10-suit Dashavatara set; shuffle gently without bending paint layers.
For a four-player Mughal session, deal twelve cards each; decide trump by the first suit led or a declared trump suit before play.
Players must follow the led suit if able; otherwise they may play trump or discard.
Highest trump wins the trick if any trump is played; otherwise the highest card of the led suit wins.
Each won trick scores one point (or count face cards if using a court-heavy house tally); highest trick total after all cards are played wins. Store cards flat.

variations.name: Dashavatara ganjifa
variations.notes: Ten-avatar suit system.

games.name: Knucklebones
games.description: Sheep or goat astragalus bones were ubiquitous ancient dice for play and divination. Children tossed and caught them; adults wagered on faces. Modern jacks are a skill descendant of the same pickup tradition.
howToPlay: Start with five astragali (or five jacks plus a small bounce ball if using modern replicas).
Scatter the pieces, toss one aloft (or bounce the ball once), and pick up one piece before catching the tossed piece or ball.
On later turns in the same round, pick up two, then three, then four pieces in one sweep while the toss or bounce is airborne.
Failing to catch or disturbing the remaining pile ends your turn; the next player restarts at picking up ones.
First player to complete the ones–twos–threes–fours sequence scores one point; play to five points. Use plastic or wooden replicas when real bones are unavailable.

variations.name: Jacks
variations.notes: Metal/plastic jacks with a bounce ball.

variations.name: Gonggi
variations.notes: Korean five-stone pickup skill game.

variations.name: Five stones (otjinori relatives)
variations.notes: Stone-toss pickup sequence games.

games.name: Yo-yo
games.civilization: Multiple; modern toy via Philippines / US
games.description: Disk-on-string toys appear in ancient art; the modern yo-yo boom traveled through Filipino makers and American brands. Sleeping, looping, and string tricks turn a simple rotor into a skill vocabulary. Contests judge difficulty and style.
howToPlay: Loop the string on your finger and wind the yo-yo.
Throw down firmly so it sleeps at the bottom.
Tug to return, or perform a trick while sleeping.
Learn sleeper, forward pass, and rock-the-baby as foundations.
Compete by trick lists or endurance sleeps.

variations.name: Bandalore
variations.notes: European fashionable disk-and-string toy.

tags: multiple; modern toy via philippines / us

games.name: Kite flying
games.description: Kites likely began in China for signaling and ceremony before becoming children’s sport worldwide. Fighter-kite cultures in Afghanistan, India, Brazil, and Japan add cutting lines and aerial combat. The toy joins craft, weather reading, and public spectacle.
howToPlay: Assemble the kite; check spars and bridle balance.
With back to the wind, have a helper hold or launch as you reel tension.
Steer with line angle; climb in steady wind.
In fighter variants, maneuver to cut an opponent’s line.
Reel in before storms; never fly near power lines.
requirements: Open windy space away from power lines

variations.name: Patang fighter kites
variations.notes: Manja abrasive line for kite battles.

variations.name: Hamamatsu festival kites
variations.notes: Giant communal kites and fighting events.

variations.name: Pipas
variations.notes: Brazilian fighter-kite street culture.

games.name: Cat's cradle
games.description: Cat’s cradle and related string figures appear from the Arctic to Oceania with startling similarity. Figures pass between hands in sequence, training spatial memory and cooperation. Anthropologists recorded hundreds of named patterns tied to stories.
howToPlay: Loop a 1–2 meter cord; Player A opens Cat’s Cradle: palms facing, strings across both hands with the palmar string crossed once.
Player B pinches the two crossed X’s, pulls them out and down, then up through the center, taking the figure onto their own hands as Soldier’s Bed (or Mattress).
Player A next takes the side strings to form Candles, then Player B takes again to form the Manger (or Cradle reverse).
If any loop slips off a finger and the figure collapses, both players restart from Player A’s opening cradle.
After one clean four-step pass (Cradle → Bed → Candles → Manger), try the sequence again or learn a solo figure such as Cup and Saucer.

variations.name: Ayatori
variations.notes: Japanese string-figure tradition.

variations.name: Hawaiian / Polynesian figures
variations.notes: String stories with local names and narratives.

games.name: Jianzi (shuttlecock kicking)
games.description: Jianzi keeps a feathered shuttlecock aloft with the feet—an accessible park sport across China and diaspora communities. Circle play builds rhythm; solo play builds count records. Korean jegichagi and Vietnamese đá cầu are the same fundamental foot-shuttlecock game.
howToPlay: Toss the shuttlecock onto your foot.
Kick with inner foot, outer foot, or knee to keep it airborne.
Count consecutive kicks; restart on a drop.
In a circle, pass to neighbors without using hands.
Agree whether hand saves are allowed (usually not).

variations.name: Jegichagi
variations.notes: Korean paper-wrapped shuttlecock kicking.

variations.name: Đá cầu
variations.notes: Vietnamese shuttlecock kicking sport.

games.name: Sepak takraw
games.description: Sepak takraw blends volleyball-like net play with foot, knee, chest, and head contacts only. Roots lie in Malay-world circle kicking (sepak raga). Overhead bicycle kicks define the modern spectacle.
howToPlay: Mark a court about 13.4 × 6.1 m with a net 1.52 m high (men’s sport height) and use a rattan or synthetic takraw ball.
Each team of three stands on its side; the server’s teammate tosses the ball for a foot serve over the net into the opponent’s court.
A side may use at most three touches with foot, knee, chest, or head before sending the ball back; hands and arms are faults.
Score one point when the ball grounds in the opponent’s court or the opponent faults (net touch with hand, four touches, out of bounds).
Play to 21 points per set (must win by 2); best of three sets decides the match.
requirements: Net and court for sport form

variations.name: Sepak raga
variations.notes: Cooperative circle keeping-up without a net.

games.name: Lacrosse
games.description: Stickball among northeastern Indigenous nations held spiritual and diplomatic weight—the Creator’s game. French observers named it lacrosse. Modern codes formalized sport rules, but cradling and scoring with a netted stick continue a deep tradition.
howToPlay: Form two teams and set goals.
Face off at center.
Carry, pass, and shoot using the stick pocket (no hand on ball in field rules).
Score by sending the ball into the goal.
Highest score at the end wins.

variations.name: Southeastern stickball
variations.notes: Double-stick ball games with distinct ritual contexts.

games.name: Mesoamerican ballgame / Ulama
games.description: The Mesoamerican ballgame used heavy rubber balls struck mainly with hips on formal courts. Ritual, politics, and sport intertwined. Modern ulama in Sinaloa continues hip-ball play as a living descendant.
howToPlay: Play ulama de cadera on a long packed-earth alley about 65 m; two teams of three to five wear hip pads and use a solid rubber ball.
Serve by bouncing the ball to a teammate who strikes it forward with the hip only—no hands, feet, or heads.
Teams volley the ball back and forth across the midline; a bounce must stay within the alley sidelines.
Score one point when the opposing team fails to return, lets the ball stop, or sends it out of the alley.
First team to 8 points wins the game (common Sinaloa street tally); rest and switch ends after each game.

variations.name: Ulama de cadera
variations.notes: Sinaloa hip-ulama continuation.

games.name: Kokeshi
games.description: Kokeshi are limbless lathe-turned wooden dolls from northern Honshu onsen towns—first souvenirs and children’s toys, now collected art. Regional schools (Naruko, Tsuchiyu, and others) differ in head joints and floral painting.
howToPlay: Display or hold the doll; there is no competitive scoring.
Children may invent nurturing stories around a kokeshi.
Collectors compare schools, signatures, and proportions.
Handle painted surfaces gently.
Use as a cultural craft object and soft play prop.

variations.name: Naruko kokeshi
variations.notes: Clicking head joint school style.

games.name: Matryoshka
games.description: Matryoshka nesting dolls were created in the 1890s at Abramtsevo workshops, influenced by nesting forms and peasant dress motifs. Each opening reveals a smaller sister—symbolizing family continuity and fertility—and became a global craft icon.
howToPlay: Open the largest doll at the seam.
Line up each inner doll by size.
Nest them closed again in order.
Invent counting or storytelling games for children.
Do not force tight seams.

games.name: Worry dolls
games.description: Guatemalan worry dolls are tiny figures to whom children tell troubles before placing them under a pillow. Folklore says the dolls carry the worries overnight—a ritual of voice and comfort more than competitive play.
howToPlay: Whisper one worry to each doll.
Place them under a pillow or in their box overnight.
In the morning, thank them and put them away.
Use as many dolls as worries (traditionally a small handful).
No scoring—personal comfort ritual.

games.name: Corn husk doll
games.description: Corn husk dolls are traditional among several Indigenous nations and later rural settlers. Faces are often left blank, with community-specific teachings about why. Making the doll is half the play.
howToPlay: Soak husks; fold and tie a head, arms, and body or skirt.
Air-dry the finished doll.
Invent caregiving play or display the figure.
Follow community protocols when learning inside a living tradition.
Keep dolls dry to prevent mold.

games.name: Bilboquet / Balero / Kendama family
games.creationYear: medieval Europe; deep Mexican roots; kendama 20th c. Japan
games.description: Cup-and-ball toys challenge hand-eye timing: swing a tethered ball into a cup or onto a spike. French bilboquet, Mexican balero, and Japanese kendama are variations of one skill family with different vocabularies of tricks.
howToPlay: Hold the handle with the ball hanging on its cord.
Swing upward and catch the ball in a cup or on the spike.
Progress to flips and named trick sequences.
Count consecutive catches.
Practice over a soft area while learning.
requirements: Cup-and-ball or spike-and-ball toy on a cord

variations.name: Balero
variations.notes: Mexican competitive cup-and-ball culture.

variations.name: Kendama
variations.notes: Multi-cup spike toy with extensive trick lexicon.

variations.name: Bilboquet
variations.notes: European parlor cup-and-ball.

games.name: Tangram
games.creationYear: c. late 18th century popular (older puzzle roots)
games.description: The tangram dissects a square into seven tans used to form silhouettes. It spread from China as a parlor craze in the 19th century. Geometric transformation and negative space are the toy’s quiet lessons.
howToPlay: Begin with all seven pieces forming a square.
Study a silhouette challenge card.
Rearrange all seven pieces to match the outline without overlaps.
Create freeform animals or letters.
Time trials optional for competitive play.

games.name: Rubik's Cube
games.description: Ernő Rubik’s cube popularized three-dimensional combination puzzles worldwide. Layer-turn mechanics hide group theory inside a colorful toy. Speedcubing culture added algorithms, hardware, and sport timing—still one puzzle at heart.
howToPlay: Scramble by turning faces randomly.
Restore each face to a solid color using layer methods or intuition.
Beginners often solve the white cross, then corners, middle edges, and last layer.
Advanced solvers memorize algorithms for speed.
Optional: time solves with a stackmat or phone timer.

variations.name: Pocket Cube (2×2)
variations.notes: Smaller order of the same mechanism.

variations.name: Revenge Cube (4×4)
variations.notes: Higher-order cuboid with reduction methods.

games.name: Building blocks
games.description: Stacking blocks are among the oldest construction toys—stone, clay, and wood stacks appear across civilizations. Froebel gifts formalized educational block play in the 19th century. The fundamental act is assembling form from modular solids.
howToPlay: Clear a stable building surface.
Stack, bridge, and cantilever blocks into towers or houses.
Agree optional challenges (tallest tower, bridge span, copy a model).
Knock down deliberately as part of play if desired.
Sort by shape when packing away.

variations.name: Froebel gifts
variations.notes: Educational block sequence for kindergartens.

variations.name: Unit blocks
variations.notes: Caroline Pratt’s modular classroom blocks.

games.name: Chunkey
games.description: Chunkey was a Mississippian plaza sport: a rolled stone disk and spears cast to predict its fall. Status, gambling, and athleticism met near mounds. Archaeology recovers finely made chunkey stones across the Midwest and South.
howToPlay: One player rolls the chunkey stone across the ground.
Others hurl poles toward where the stone will stop.
Score by closeness when the stone rests.
Rotate roles; play to an agreed point total.
Keep spectators clear of the throw path.

games.name: Palín
games.description: Palín (chueca) is a Mapuche stick-and-ball game with communal and ritual importance. Teams drive a ball toward goals on a long pitch. It remains a marker of Mapuche gathering and identity.
howToPlay: Mark a long field with goals at each end.
Start the ball at center between teams.
Strike with sticks toward your goal—no dangerous swings at people.
Score when the ball crosses the goal space.
Play to agreed points; honor ceremonial openings when hosted traditionally.

games.name: Tug of war
games.description: Tug of war appears in harvest rites, school sports, and village festivals worldwide. Some East Asian and Pacific forms carry cosmological meanings of seasonal balance. Two teams, one rope—an elemental coordination contest.
howToPlay: Mark a center line and team foul lines.
Teams grip evenly; avoid wrapping the rope around limbs in sport rules.
On a signal, pull with short coordinated heaves.
Win by pulling the center marker across your line.
Stop immediately if someone slips dangerously.

variations.name: Japanese tsunahiki festival forms
variations.notes: Communal ropes in ritual calendar events.

variations.name: Korean juldarigi
variations.notes: Village tug rites around festivals.

games.name: Hide-and-seek
games.description: Hide-and-seek is a near-universal children’s game with countless local names and counting rhymes. It rehearses stealth, spatial memory, and the social thrill of being found. Architecture—from kasbah alleys to apartment stairwells—reshapes strategy.
howToPlay: Pick one seeker and a home base (tree, wall, or stoop); set hard bounds—no street, no locked rooms.
The seeker faces the base and counts aloud to 50 while others hide inside the bounds.
The seeker shouts “Ready or not, here I come,” then tags hiders by touch; tagged players walk to a jail spot beside home base.
A free hider may dash to base, touch it, and call “Free [name]!” to release one jailed player; if the seeker tags them on the way, they go to jail.
When all hiders are jailed, or after five minutes, the first player tagged becomes the next seeker.

variations.name: Sardines
variations.notes: Inverse hiding: one hides, others join the hiding spot.

games.name: Hopscotch
games.description: Hopping grids for tossed markers appear across continents with local shapes and rhymes. Balance, turn-taking, and pavement chalk art meet in one simple race through numbered cells.
howToPlay: Draw a numbered hopscotch grid.
Toss a marker into the next square; it must land cleanly inside.
Hop through on one foot, skipping the occupied square.
Retrieve the marker on the return without faults.
First to complete all numbers wins.

variations.name: Rayuela
variations.notes: Spanish-language hopscotch naming and grid variants.

variations.name: Marelle
variations.notes: French hopscotch grids and schoolyard rules.

games.name: Marbles
games.description: Marble rings are nearly universal children’s gaming. Clay, stone, and later glass spheres are knuckle-shot to knock targets from a circle. ‘Keepsies’ versus friendlies decide whether winners keep captured marbles.
howToPlay: Draw a circle and place target marbles inside.
Knuckle-shoot from the edge to knock targets out.
Captured marbles score or are kept depending on agreed stakes.
If your shooter remains in-ring, many rules allow another shot from there.
Clear the ring or reach a point goal to win.

variations.name: Ringer
variations.notes: Formal marble-tournament circle rules.

games.name: Spinning top
games.description: Tops are among humanity’s oldest mechanical toys, excavated from Ur to the Indus and beyond. String-launch and whip-sustained forms support endurance contests and combat. Local names differ; the physics lesson is shared.
howToPlay: Wind string around the body or prepare a whip.
Launch with a smooth pull so the tip spins on hard ground.
Optionally whip to add energy.
Compete for longest spin or for knocking out rivals.
Repair worn tips as needed.

variations.name: Trompo
variations.notes: Cord-thrown combat and trick tops.

variations.name: Koma
variations.notes: Japanese arena and festival tops.

variations.name: Lattoo
variations.notes: South Asian whipping / string tops.

variations.name: Ttoli
variations.notes: Korean whipping top.

games.name: Hnefatafl
games.description: Hnefatafl is a Norse asymmetric hunt: a king and defenders try to escape attackers on a grid. Variants spread across Viking worlds. Balance of forces and throne squares define tense endgames.
howToPlay: Play Copenhagen Hnefatafl on an 11×11 board: place the king on the center throne with 12 defenders in a cross; place 24 attackers in the four edge camps.
Attackers move first. Every piece slides any number of empty squares like a rook; none may jump.
Capture an enemy by sandwiching it between two of your pieces on a rank or file (custodial capture); the throne and corner squares can help bracket.
Attackers win by capturing the king on two opposite sides (or against the throne/edge as a second side). Defenders win if the king reaches any of the four corner sanctuary squares.
Pieces may not stop on the throne except the king; attackers may not occupy the corners.

variations.name: Tablut
variations.notes: Linnaeus recorded Sámi tablut—same tafl family.

variations.name: Brandub
variations.notes: Irish tafl relative on a smaller board.

games.name: Fox and Geese
games.description: Asymmetric hunt on a cross: geese try to corner a fox that leaps to capture. Related to many predator-prey boards worldwide—the European parlor form is catalogued here with cousins as variations.
howToPlay: Place geese on one end and the fox centrally or opposite per rules.
Geese move first or second by agreement; they walk without jumping.
Fox may jump adjacent geese to capture.
Geese win by immobilizing the fox; fox wins by capturing enough geese.
Use a modern printed fox-and-geese board if historic boards are unavailable.

variations.name: Cercar la Liebre
variations.notes: Hare-hunting asymmetric relative.

variations.name: Hyena game
variations.notes: Spiral predator-prey race cousin.

games.name: Go Bang / Gomoku
games.description: Five-in-a-row on a Go-like grid is an ancient East Asian pastime formalized as gomoku and renju. Distinct from Go's territory scoring—the goal is a straight five.
howToPlay: Black places first on an intersection.
Players alternate placing one stone.
First to form five consecutive stones in a line wins.
Sport renju adds opening restrictions for balance.
Play on a dedicated gomoku board or a Go board.

variations.name: Renju
variations.notes: Balanced competitive ruleset for five-in-a-row.

games.name: Reversi / Othello
games.description: Reversi flips sandwiched discs to claim majority color. Othello standardized modern branding and opening. A pure placement-and-flip contest with explosive endgame swings.
howToPlay: Place four discs in the center in the standard Othello opening.
Black places first on a square that flips at least one white disc.
Flip all sandwiched opponent discs in every direction.
A player unable to flip passes; when both cannot move, count discs.
Majority color wins.

variations.name: Othello
variations.notes: Trademarked modern standardization of reversi-like play.

games.name: Scrabble
games.description: Scrabble assigns point values to letters on a crossword-style grid with premium squares. Born from American crossword culture, it became a global word sport with language-specific sets.
howToPlay: Draw seven tiles; place first word through the center star.
Build new words connecting to existing letters crossword-style.
Score letter values times premiums; tally each turn.
Draw back to seven tiles after each play.
Highest score when tiles run out and one player empties their rack wins.

games.name: Snakes and Ladders
games.creationYear: c. 2nd century BCE–19th century CE forms
games.description: Paramapada sopanam / gyan chaupar taught karma with virtues as ladders and vices as snakes. British Snakes and Ladders secularized the race for children—same fundamental up-and-down morality track.
howToPlay: Place tokens off the board; roll to enter.
Move forward by the die.
Land at a ladder base to climb; land on a snake head to slide down.
Exact roll may be required to finish.
First to the final square wins.
requirements: Grid board with snakes and ladders

variations.name: Gyan Chaupar
variations.notes: Didactic ancestor with virtues and vices labeled.

variations.name: Chutes and Ladders
variations.notes: American Milton Bradley branding of the same race.

games.name: Monopoly
games.description: Property-trading race games critique or celebrate real-estate capitalism. Magie's Landlord's Game preceded Parker Brothers' Monopoly. Local editions map world cities onto the same buy-rent-bankrupt loop.
howToPlay: Each player starts with allotted cash and a token at Go.
Roll dice, move, and buy unowned properties you land on—or pay rent.
Build houses/hotels on complete color sets.
Manage mortgages and trades.
Last player not bankrupt wins.

variations.name: The Landlord's Game
variations.notes: Elizabeth Magie's teaching ancestor.

games.name: Jenga
games.description: Jenga formalizes the ancient thrill of removing pieces from a stack without collapse. Leslie Scott marketed the tower game globally; the physical puzzle is one shared stack for all players.
howToPlay: Build the tower in alternating crosswise layers of three.
On your turn, remove one block below the incomplete top layer using one hand.
Place it on the top to complete or continue layers.
The player who topples the tower loses (or the prior player wins).
Rebuild to play again.

games.name: Diabolo
games.description: The Chinese kongzhu / diabolo spins on a string between sticks—tosses, accelerations, and suicides form a circus vocabulary. European circuses adopted and renamed it diabolo.
howToPlay: Start the spool rocking on the string.
Accelerate with alternating stick motions.
Toss and catch; attempt orbit tricks.
Count consecutive catches or trick scores.
Use open space clear of lamps and faces.

variations.name: Kongzhu
variations.notes: Chinese name and folk/circus tradition for the same spool toy.

games.name: Kapu kuapu / Jackstraws / Spillikins
games.description: Pick-up sticks (spillikins, jackstraws) drop in a tangle; players extract sticks without moving others. Color values score. A quiet parlor test of fine motor control.
howToPlay: Hold sticks upright in a bundle and release to scramble.
Players alternately pull one stick without wiggling others.
If others move, your turn ends (and the stick may return).
Score by stick colors/values.
Highest score when the pile is cleared wins.

variations.name: Mikado
variations.notes: Named commercial pick-up sticks set.

games.name: Mehen
games.description: Mehen, the coiled serpent game, appears in early dynastic Egypt. Play moved along a spiral serpent toward the center; exact rules are fragmentary, but the board's sacred animal form is clear.
howToPlay: Place pieces at the serpent's tail.
Throw sticks to advance inward along the spiral.
Resolve interactions when sharing segments per a chosen reconstruction.
Reaching the center may reverse the path outward.
First to complete the journey wins in most reconstructions.

games.name: Buckingham Palace toy soldiers aside: Toy soldiers
games.description: Cast or printed miniature soldiers supported war play and later wargaming. German tin makers and British hollow-casts spread sets worldwide. Play ranges from simple line battles to rule-heavy simulations.
howToPlay: Array two equal forces of at least ten figures each on opposite ends of a table or sand tray; place one flag token behind each line.
On a turn, move up to three of your figures up to one hand-span forward, sideways, or diagonally.
If a figure ends within one finger-width of an enemy, roll one six-sided die: 4–6 removes the enemy; 1–3 misses. Remove casualties to a dead pile.
Capture the opponent’s flag by ending a move on its square, or eliminate every enemy figure, to win.
Store figures upright in a box with tissue so paint and bayonets do not chip.

variations.name: Tin flats
variations.notes: Early mass-painted flat tin soldiers.

games.name: Tea set toy
games.originCountry: United Kingdom / Europe / East Asia porcelain play
games.description: Miniature tea sets let children rehearse hospitality rituals. Porcelain and tin versions tracked adult tea cultures from Britain to Japan. Social scripts—pouring, offering, thanking—are the real ruleset.
howToPlay: Set places for dolls or friends.
Pour (real or imaginary) tea without tipping cups.
Practice serving order and polite phrases.
Wash and put away as part of play.
No score—etiquette role-play.
tags: united kingdom / europe / east asia porcelain play

games.name: Slinky
games.description: The Slinky converts potential energy into end-over-end stair walking. A happy accident of naval spring engineering became a global desk and stair toy.
howToPlay: Place the Slinky on a stair tread.
Tip the top coil to the next lower step.
Watch it walk; restart when it tumbles.
On flat desks, rock it between hands as a wave.
Avoid overstretching coils permanently.

games.name: Frisbee / flying disc
games.description: Flying discs formalized beach and park tossing; ultimate and disc golf added sport frames. The fundamental toy is a hand-thrown gliding plate.
howToPlay: Grip the disc with fingers under the rim.
Throw flat with a spin; face the target.
Catch with two hands when learning.
Play catch, ultimate scores, or disc-golf holes.
Mind wind and bystanders.

games.name: Hacky sack / footbag
games.originCountry: United States / global; older Asian footbags
games.civilization: Modern global; ancient Chinese cuju relatives for feet
games.creationYear: 1970s CE popular footbag; older kickbags centuries
games.description: Keeping a small bag aloft with feet echoes older Eurasian kickbag play. Circle 'sunny' sessions emphasize style and sharing over scoring.
howToPlay: Drop the bag to a foot and kick gently upward.
Use feet, knees, and thighs—no hands.
In a circle, pass to neighbors.
Count consecutive kicks.
Restart together after a drop.

variations.name: Chinese shuttlecock/footbag relatives
variations.notes: Older kick-keeping traditions related in spirit.

tags: united states / global; older asian footbags
modern global; ancient chinese cuju relatives for feet

games.name: Boomerang
games.description: Returning boomerangs are precision-carved throwing sticks from Aboriginal Australian traditions, also used in hunting forms that do not return. Tourist sport boomerangs simplify the returning toy; cultural knowledge of designs remains with communities.
howToPlay: Use only in huge clear fields with no people downrange.
Grip and throw at the angle taught for that shape.
Watch the return path; do not snatch blindly.
Let it land if unsure.
Learn from knowledgeable throwers; respect design ownership.

games.name: Poi
games.description: Māori poi swung in dance train wrist rhythm and storytelling. Modern fire and performance poi extend the toy globally; traditional contexts remain cultural practice.
howToPlay: Hold cords with weights clear of people.
Swing in simple side circles to a beat.
Add patterns as skill grows.
In cultural performance, follow song and choreography.
Use fire poi only with professional safety practice.
requirements: Poi (flax or modern weights on cords)

games.name: Surakarta
games.description: Surakarta is a Javanese capture game where pieces travel circuits around colored loops. Captures follow the loops rather than simple jumps—an elegant regional strategy toy.
howToPlay: Array pieces on your side of the board.
Move to adjacent empty points.
Capture by traveling along a circuit loop onto an enemy.
Removed pieces leave gaps that reshape routes.
Capture all enemies to win.

games.name: Dakon
games.description: Dakon is a Javanese congkak-family sowing board, often elaborately carved. It is presented as a named regional standard within mancala while remaining one sowing family.
howToPlay: Use a boat board with seven small cups per side plus one large store (lumbung) at each end; place seven seeds in every small cup.
On your turn, scoop one of your cups and sow one seed clockwise into each following cup, including your store but skipping the opponent’s store.
If the last seed lands in your store, sow again immediately from any of your cups that still hold seeds (relay turn).
If the last seed lands in an empty cup on your side, capture that seed and all seeds in the opposite cup into your store.
When one player cannot move, remaining seeds go to the owner of those cups; most seeds in store wins.

variations.name: Congkak
variations.notes: Closely related Malay boat-board sowing game—same family.

games.name: Sungka
games.description: Sungka is the Filipino boat-shaped sowing game, cousin to congkak. Boards are household heirlooms; play mixes speed sowing with capture timing.
howToPlay: Seat two players at a sungka board with seven small cups (bahay) per side and one head store (ulo) each; place seven cowries or seeds in every bahay.
Scoop all seeds from one of your bahay and sow counterclockwise one-by-one into each following cup, including your ulo but skipping the opponent’s ulo.
If the last seed lands in your ulo, take another turn; if it lands in an empty bahay on your side, capture the opposite bahay’s seeds into your ulo.
A player who empties their side early waits while the opponent may still sow; continue until neither side has seeds left in bahay.
Count cowries in each ulo; the higher store wins.

variations.name: Congkak
variations.notes: Malay relative—variation within sowing boat boards.

games.name: Infant rattle — Egypt
games.description: Rattles are among the oldest sound toys. In Egypt, Ancient Egypt caregivers have long sealed seeds or pebbles in gourd, clay, basketry, or wood to reward infant grasping and rhythm. The rattle is both sensory toy and, in some places, a protective charm sound.
howToPlay: In Egypt, offer a sealed Ancient Egypt rattle (gourd, clay, wood, or basketry with seeds or pebbles) within the infant’s supervised reach.
Shake once slowly so the child hears a clear cause-and-effect sound, then pause for them to grasp.
Allow grasping, gentle shaking, and dropping onto a soft mat; block mouthing if the shell cracks or finishes flake.
Sing or speak a short Ancient Egypt lullaby or counting rhyme from Egypt in time with three to five shakes.
After each session, check seams, plugs, and loose bits; retire the toy if seeds can spill.
requirements: Hollow rattle with seeds, pebbles, or bells

howToPlay: In Mongolia, offer a sealed Mongol steppe rattle (gourd, clay, wood, or basketry with seeds or pebbles) within the infant’s supervised reach.
Shake once slowly so the child hears a clear cause-and-effect sound, then pause for them to grasp.
Allow grasping, gentle shaking, and dropping onto a soft mat; block mouthing if the shell cracks or finishes flake.
Sing or speak a short Mongol steppe lullaby or counting rhyme from Mongolia in time with three to five shakes.
After each session, check seams, plugs, and loose bits; retire the toy if seeds can spill.
requirements: Hollow rattle with seeds, pebbles, or bells

howToPlay: In Ireland, offer a sealed Irish rattle (gourd, clay, wood, or basketry with seeds or pebbles) within the infant’s supervised reach.
Shake once slowly so the child hears a clear cause-and-effect sound, then pause for them to grasp.
Allow grasping, gentle shaking, and dropping onto a soft mat; block mouthing if the shell cracks or finishes flake.
Sing or speak a short Irish lullaby or counting rhyme from Ireland in time with three to five shakes.
After each session, check seams, plugs, and loose bits; retire the toy if seeds can spill.
requirements: Hollow rattle with seeds, pebbles, or bells

howToPlay: In New Zealand, offer a sealed Māori rattle (gourd, clay, wood, or basketry with seeds or pebbles) within the infant’s supervised reach.
Shake once slowly so the child hears a clear cause-and-effect sound, then pause for them to grasp.
Allow grasping, gentle shaking, and dropping onto a soft mat; block mouthing if the shell cracks or finishes flake.
Sing or speak a short Māori lullaby or counting rhyme from New Zealand in time with three to five shakes.
After each session, check seams, plugs, and loose bits; retire the toy if seeds can spill.
requirements: Hollow rattle with seeds, pebbles, or bells

games.name: Clay or wood whistle toy — Egypt
games.description: Small whistles—bird-shaped clay, carved wood, reed—appear in markets and archaeological layers tied to Ancient Egypt life in Egypt. Children use them as voice-amplifying toys; some double as festival noisemakers. Sound play teaches breath and pitch playfully.
howToPlay: Hold a clay, wood, or reed whistle made in the Ancient Egypt craft style of Egypt; keep finger holes and the windway clear.
Blow a steady stream for two seconds to find one clear tone before trying short chirps.
Alternate three short calls and one long note; count successful clear tones aloud.
Play call-and-response with a partner: one player blows a rhythm from Egypt street or festival play, the other copies it.
Wash or wipe the mouthpiece between players; do not share if anyone is ill.

howToPlay: Hold a clay, wood, or reed whistle made in the Persian craft style of Iran; keep finger holes and the windway clear.
Blow a steady stream for two seconds to find one clear tone before trying short chirps.
Alternate three short calls and one long note; count successful clear tones aloud.
Play call-and-response with a partner: one player blows a rhythm from Iran street or festival play, the other copies it.
Wash or wipe the mouthpiece between players; do not share if anyone is ill.

games.name: Animal pull toy — Egypt
games.description: Wheeled animals and pull-along figures are documented from classical antiquity through village woodcrafts in Egypt. Ancient Egypt artisans shape horses, birds, or oxen that teach walking toddlers about traction and companionship in motion.
howToPlay: Tie a short cord to the nose or yoke of a wheeled Ancient Egypt animal figure from Egypt; leave enough slack for a toddler’s stride.
Walk five to ten steps on a clear floor so wheels or runners follow without tipping.
Make one gentle left turn and one right turn; stop if the axle binds or the cord jerks the toy airborne.
Narrate a short parade or market delivery story using animals familiar in Egypt (horse, ox, bird, or camel as fits the figure).
Coil the cord after play and store the toy upright so wheels stay round.

games.name: Toy bow or dart play set — Egypt
games.description: Scaled hunting toys let children in Egypt rehearse skills celebrated by Ancient Egypt adults—archery, spear-thorn darts, or blowpipe aim—using safer materials. Targets on straw, wood, or drawn circles turn martial technique into scored play.
howToPlay: Outdoors in Egypt, set a straw, wood, or chalk target with a backstop; clear people and animals for at least five paces downrange.
Nock a soft arrow or load a foam/cork dart; keep the tip pointed at the ground until ready.
Use a calm Ancient Egypt stance—feet apart, eyes on the center ring—and release one shot at a time.
Score 3 points for the center, 2 for the middle ring, 1 for the outer; first to 15 points wins a round.
Never aim at people or animals; collect every projectile before the next turn.

games.name: Pocket skill stones — Egypt
games.description: Beyond the shared knucklebones family, Egypt has local stone-and-seed skill sequences shaped by Ancient Egypt childhood—different throws, chants, and difficulty ladders on the same pickup principle, recorded here as a regional practice entry when chants and sequences are locally distinct.
howToPlay: Sit on flat ground in Egypt with five small stones or seeds used in Ancient Egypt children’s pickup play.
Scatter all five lightly, then toss one skyward and pick up exactly one stone before catching the tossed stone.
On the next turns, pick up two, then three, then the last group of remaining stones in one sweep while the toss is aloft.
Drop or fail to catch ends your turn; the next player restarts at ones.
First player to finish the ones–twos–threes–fours ladder while saying a short Ancient Egypt count or chant from Egypt wins.

games.name: Shadow figures play — Egypt
games.description: Shadow play—hand animals or leather puppets—has entertained nights in Egypt within Ancient Egypt storytelling. Light and silhouette turn gesture into theater. Some regions elevated this into formal puppet arts; children's hand shadows remain the toy form.
howToPlay: In a dim room in Egypt, place a lamp or candle so hands cast sharp shadows on a blank wall about one arm’s length away.
Form one animal or person with fingers; move slowly for three seconds so the outline stays readable.
Narrate a one-minute Ancient Egypt folk scene (market, animal chase, or hero greeting) while the shadow acts.
Optional: cut a cardboard figure, tape it to a stick, and replay the same scene with crisper edges.
End by letting each child invent one new creature and name it before the lamp is put out.

games.name: Local kite craft — Egypt
games.description: While kite flying is one global family, Egypt's Ancient Egypt makers developed distinctive shapes, papers, bridles, and festival uses. This entry highlights that local craft tradition as a regional kite practice under the wider kite sky.
howToPlay: Build or buy a paper or cloth kite in a shape used by Ancient Egypt makers in Egypt (diamond, box, bird, or fighter flat).
Check that both bridle legs are equal and the spar joints are tight before you walk to the field.
Stand with the wind at your back in open ground; have a helper release the kite as you take three steps and feed five to ten meters of line.
Steer by tension: pull to climb, ease to dive; land by walking toward the kite while reeling.
Never fly near power lines, airports, or storms—common safety rules for festival kite days in Egypt.

howToPlay: Build or buy a paper or cloth kite in a shape used by Southern African peoples makers in South Africa (diamond, box, bird, or fighter flat).
Check that both bridle legs are equal and the spar joints are tight before you walk to the field.
Stand with the wind at your back in open ground; have a helper release the kite as you take three steps and feed five to ten meters of line.
Steer by tension: pull to climb, ease to dive; land by walking toward the kite while reeling.
Never fly near power lines, airports, or storms—common safety rules for festival kite days in South Africa.

Repair tears with needle and thread as part of play rather than discarding the doll.
No points are scored—nurture play ends when the child packs the doll into a small basket or box used in Georgia households.

Dress the doll in miniature wraps, sash, or embroidered scraps that echo everyday Māori clothing in New Zealand.
Act out at least three caregiving scenes: wake, feed, and put to sleep.
Repair tears with needle and thread as part of play rather than discarding the doll.
No points are scored—nurture play ends when the child packs the doll into a small basket or box used in New Zealand households.

games.name: Sewn cloth or hide ball — Egypt
games.description: Before industrial rubber, Ancient Egypt communities in Egypt stuffed and sewed balls from hide, cloth, or plant fiber. Catch, kick, and circle games grew around these objects. The ball's make is as cultural as the rules.
howToPlay: Form a circle of four or more players in a clear yard in Egypt; use one sewn cloth, palm-fiber, or hide ball.
Toss underhand to the neighbor on your right; Ancient Egypt circle play scores one point for each clean catch.
A drop removes that player from the circle (or gives the thrower one point if you play pairs).
When three players remain, speed up to a one-second hold before passing.
Last player in the circle wins; restart with everyone after one champion round.
requirements: Sewn cloth, palm, or hide ball

Toss underhand to the neighbor on your right; Anatolian / Ottoman circle play scores one point for each clean catch.
A drop removes that player from the circle (or gives the thrower one point if you play pairs).

Last player in the circle wins; restart with everyone after one champion round.

howToPlay: Wind a cord clockwise around a carved Andean top from Ecuador, or ready a short whip cord if the tip is meant for whipping.
Plant your feet on hard earth or stone; pull the cord smooth and level so the tip bites and spins.
For whip tops, tap the shoulder of the top lightly to keep it upright for a timed spin.
In a contest, longest continuous spin wins; or play combat where the first top knocked flat loses.

howToPlay: Make a loop of cord about the span of your outstretched arms so it fits both hands with slight slack.
Open on both thumbs and little fingers in the starting position taught for Indonesian archipelago figures in Indonesia.
Pick, drop, and transfer strings until you hold one named figure (animal, tool, or star) for three seconds.
Say the figure’s Indonesian archipelago name or a one-sentence story tied to Indonesia while holding the shape.
Teach that single figure to a partner before starting a second pattern.

games.name: Folk race board (local) — Egypt
games.description: Cross-and-circle and path race boards appear in many lands. In Egypt, Ancient Egypt players used shells, sticks, or knucklebones to race markers home—cousins to pachisi-like structures but with local track shapes and safe-space customs recorded as a regional folk race board.
howToPlay: Seat 2–4 players at a path or cross-and-circle board used in Egypt; each gets four markers in a starting nest.
Throw two casting sticks, four cowrie shells, or one die—whatever Ancient Egypt sets use—and total the pips or “mouth-up” shells.
Enter a marker only on a throw of the highest single result (for example 4 sticks or a 6); then advance that many spaces.
Landing on an opponent’s single marker sends it back to its nest; stacked markers are safe.
First player to move all four markers around the track and into the home column wins.

games.name: Local pit-and-seed sowing — Egypt
games.description: Where sowing games took root in Egypt, Ancient Egypt boards show distinctive cup counts, relay rules, and wood shapes. They belong to the mancala family yet deserve regional entries when board geometry and capture customs are locally standardized.
howToPlay: Use a 2×6 board (twelve small pits plus one store per side) common in Ancient Egypt sowing play in Egypt; place four seeds in each small pit.
On your turn, scoop every seed from one pit on your side and sow one seed into each following pit counterclockwise, including your store but skipping the opponent’s store.
If the last seed lands in your empty pit and the opposite pit holds seeds, capture those opposite seeds into your store.
If the last seed lands in your store, take another turn; otherwise play passes.
When one side’s pits are empty, the opponent puts remaining seeds in their store; most seeds in store wins.
requirements: Cup board or pits in earth

games.name: Blind man's tag / call games — Egypt
games.description: Blindfolded seeking games—call-and-dodge variants—appear across Ancient Egypt parties and children's gatherings in Egypt. Sound, stillness, and empathy for the blinded player structure the fun.
howToPlay: Clear toys and furniture from a bounded room or yard in Egypt; mark walls or chalk lines as out-of-bounds.
Blindfold one seeker and spin them twice; sighted players must stay inside the bounds.
Sighted players may call a short Ancient Egypt nickname or clap once every five seconds so the seeker has sound cues.
The seeker tags by touch; the tagged player becomes the next seeker.
Stop the round immediately if anyone near stairs or hard edges; remove the blindfold before leaving the space.

games.name: Stilts or balance poles — Egypt
games.description: Stilts appear as festival tools and children's balance toys in Egypt. Ancient Egypt makers raise walkers on bamboo, wood, or recycled cans. Racing and trick-stepping turn elevation into play.
howToPlay: Mount bamboo, wood, or tin-can stilts built in the Ancient Egypt style of Egypt with a spotter holding your elbow.
Take ten small steps on level ground while looking forward, not down at the footrests.
Race a marked ten-meter line, or walk a chalk zigzag without a footrest touching the ground.
Dismount by stepping backward onto clear ground with the spotter ready.
Check cords, cans, and footrest bindings before every session; replace frayed ties.
requirements: Pair of stilts or tin-can stilts

games.name: Leaf or bark boat racing — Egypt
games.description: Miniature boat races using leaves, bark, or corncobs delight children near water in Egypt. Ancient Egypt play turns currents into tracks and craft into engineering experiments.
howToPlay: Fold a broad leaf or carve a bark/cork hull that floats—materials children gather near water in Egypt.
Mark a start and finish about two meters apart in a basin or gentle gutter current.
On a shared count of three in any Ancient Egypt counting words, release all boats together; no pushing after release.
First boat to touch the finish line wins the heat; run best of three heats.
Retrieve every leaf, twig, and cork; leave the water clear of trash.
requirements: Leaves, bark, or cork for hulls

games.name: Table flick football / paper soccer — Egypt
games.description: Flick games that simulate football/soccer on a tabletop spread through schools in Egypt, layered onto older finger-flicking toy habits in Ancient Egypt childhood. Goals are books or drawn posts; tournaments can be fierce.
howToPlay: On a clear table in Egypt, mark each goal with two small gaps about three finger-widths wide (books or tape posts).
Place a coin, button, or crumpled paper ball on the center line.
Players alternate one finger-flick; no covering the ball with a palm—common Ancient Egypt school-desk rule.
A goal scores when the ball fully crosses between the posts; play to five goals.
If the ball leaves the table, the opponent places it back one hand-span from the edge and flicks next.

Place a coin, button, or crumpled paper ball on the center line.
Players alternate one finger-flick; no covering the ball with a palm—common Finnish school-desk rule.
A goal scores when the ball fully crosses between the posts; play to five goals.
If the ball leaves the table, the opponent places it back one hand-span from the edge and flicks next.

games.name: Local riddle exchange — Egypt
games.description: Riddle exchanges in Egypt preserve Ancient Egypt metaphor, ecology, and humor. Posing and solving under time pressure is a mind toy requiring no manufactured equipment.
howToPlay: One player poses a riddle drawn from Ancient Egypt oral tradition in Egypt (animals, tools, weather, or food metaphors).
Others have one minute and up to three guesses.
A correct solver scores one point and poses the next riddle; if no one solves, the poser scores one point and chooses the next poser.
Optional playful forfeit for three wrong guesses: clap a rhythm or name five animals from ${c}.
First to five points wins the exchange.

games.name: Cord & knot puzzle toy — Egypt
games.description: Disentanglement puzzles of cord, rings, and wood appear as market toys and blacksmith curiosities around Egypt. Ancient Egypt players learn topology by touch—release a ring without forcing, then reassemble.
howToPlay: Study a cord-and-ring or wire puzzle sold or forged around Egypt; note which loop is the piece you must free.
Move loops only through openings that already exist—do not bend metal or force wood.
Free the target ring or block by a legal path; Ancient Egypt market puzzles are solved when that piece separates cleanly.
Reassemble every loop to the exact starting state before claiming the solve.
Time your solve, then challenge a friend to beat that time with the same path.

howToPlay: Study a cord-and-ring or wire puzzle sold or forged around Russia; note which loop is the piece you must free.
Move loops only through openings that already exist—do not bend metal or force wood.
Free the target ring or block by a legal path; Russian market puzzles are solved when that piece separates cleanly.
Reassemble every loop to the exact starting state before claiming the solve.
Time your solve, then challenge a friend to beat that time with the same path.

games.name: Miniature household play set — Egypt
games.description: Tiny household tools—clay pans, woven mats, doll furniture—support role-play of adult domestic life in Ancient Egypt childhoods in Egypt. Archaeology and ethnography both find these teaching toys.
howToPlay: Arrange miniature pots, mats, and dolls into a small hearth or room layout familiar in Egypt.
Assign roles (cook, guest, child) to dolls or players before the scene starts.
Act out one cooking scene, one market or visiting scene, and one bedtime scene drawn from Ancient Egypt daily life.
Add one new prop each week (ladle, basket, or stool) and reuse it in the next story.
Pack all pieces into one box after play so the set stays complete.
